I did what Farida told me to do, and I'm so glad.
"Kabir" and I matched on the dating app two weeks ago. Perfect photos, perfect messages. An architect in Dubai. He said I was the most beautiful woman he'd ever spoken to.
Farida said, "Before you get any deeper, video call. Early. And do an image search." So on Thursday I asked for a quick video call. He said his camera was broken. Friday, I asked again. He got angry. "Don't you trust me? After everything?"
That anger was the answer, really. Farida sat with me while I did a reverse image search. His photos belonged to a fitness model in Brazil.
Tonight he asked me to send a "private" photo to prove I trust him. I blocked and reported him instead.
I'm sad. I liked those messages. But a real person would have just switched on the camera.
Ayesha

I'm Tenzin, and it took me six weeks to tell anyone what happened.
Mira and I met on a language exchange app. She said she was a nurse in Canada. We talked every night for three months. She knew about my exams, my grandmother, my favourite songs. I felt, for the first time, really loved.
Then she wrote that her mother was in hospital and her bank account was frozen. She was crying in the voice notes. She needed ₹40,000 for surgery. I had my scholarship money. I didn't think. I just sent it.
Then another emergency. Then another. After the third, she disappeared.
I was so ashamed. I'm a science student. How could I be so stupid? I didn't tell my parents. I didn't report it.
It was my roommate Anirban who noticed I wasn't eating. When I finally told him, he said, "They do this professionally. You're not stupid." He came with me to the cyber police station the next day.

I'm Alka, and I've known Nazia since school. Over three months, I watched something that scared me.
Every few weeks she asked to borrow a little money. Then I saw her at the bank, sending money abroad. She told me it was for Daniel, an engineer on an oil rig she'd met online. His salary was stuck. His daughter was sick. His equipment was held at customs.
She'd never met him.

So over coffee I asked questions. "Has he ever video called? Has he ever sent you anything? Why does every problem need money?" She got quiet. Then she said, "He always has a reason."
I showed her an article about scam centres that work in shifts, with scripts. Professionals. She read it twice.
She didn't stop that day. But she agreed to come with me to the cyber cell on Saturday.

Bank teller's note, Friday. Written by Urmila, counter 3.
Avni, a regular customer, came in today for her fourth international transfer this month. Each time, a larger amount, to a different name. Today she seemed anxious and was checking her phone constantly.
I didn't refuse or lecture. I asked, gently, "Is this for family?" She said it was for her fiancé, a doctor working abroad, whom she hasn't met yet. He needs help with a legal fee.
I asked, "Has he ever asked you to keep this secret?" She hesitated, then nodded.
I explained, as kindly as I could, that we see this often, that these are organised groups who build a persona over months, and that she is not foolish for believing it. I showed her our bank's scam warning leaflet.
With her agreement, we paused the transfer and I called our fraud team, who spoke to her in the back office. She left with the cyber police helpline number written on her hand.

Wasim sent money again today. That's the fifth time since March.

I read online that these scams are run like companies, with teams, scripts and targets. Wasim isn't stupid. He's up against a whole business.

Uday

I'm Kunal, and I lost ₹3,000 I didn't have, in my final year.
I'd been job-hunting for months. My father had retired, and I felt I needed to earn fast. Then a message came on a messaging app: "Part-time online work. ₹1,500 a day. Only one hour. Registration: ₹3,000, fully refundable."
It sounded too good. But I was so desperate that I wanted it to be true. The woman on the phone was polite and professional. She sent an official-looking offer letter with a logo.
I paid. Then they asked for a "security deposit" and my bank login "for salary setup." That's when my stomach dropped.
I called my friend Nirmala, whose brother works in a bank. She said, "Don't send anything more. Block them. Call your bank now." We reported it on the cyber crime portal that night.
I felt stupid for weeks. Now I tell everyone: if they charge you to hire you, it isn't a job.

Then they asked her to pay a "document verification fee" and to let them use her bank account "to receive client payments," with a small commission for her.
Ganga refused both. She told them, "Real employers don't charge to hire. And no one uses my bank account or ID."
She reported the offer on the cyber crime portal and came to us to warn other students. We've shared her checklist with the whole final year.

I'm Kunal, and last year I learned how the trap works from the inside.
My friend Kalyani added me to a trading group. The screenshots were unbelievable. Members posted "₹50k profit today!" with party emojis. A mentor called "Sir" gave tips every morning. Returns were "guaranteed."
I started with ₹5,000. In two weeks it showed ₹9,000. I withdrew ₹3,000, and it came straight to my bank. That was the moment I trusted it completely.
So I added ₹1.5 lakh. My savings. Then more, when they said my account needed "tax clearance" to withdraw.
Then the group went silent. The app stopped opening. Kalyani lost money too.
I felt stupid and scared. But the first small payout was designed to make me feel exactly what I felt: safe. Now, whenever someone says "guaranteed," I think of that ₹3,000. It was the most expensive money I ever received.

Financial literacy counsellor's note, community centre, Saturday. Written by Noor.
Jeevan came in today with a printout. A colleague had offered him a place in an "exclusive gold trading scheme": guaranteed twelve percent a month, entry closing Monday, and "don't share this with too many people."
What impressed me was what he had already done. He hadn't paid anything. He had searched the scheme's name on the official regulator's website: not registered. He had asked the colleague for a company registration number: no answer.
He said, "It sounded too good, and too fast, and too quiet. So I wanted someone independent to look." I confirmed his findings and explained that real investments always carry some risk and aren't sold with secrecy.
He decided not to invest, and he's going to tell the colleague why, gently, in case the colleague has put in money too. We also reported the scheme to the cyber police together.

Pranav hadn't slept properly in two weeks. His ₹4 lakh, five years of savings for a flat, had vanished into a trading app that one morning simply stopped opening.

Mridul didn't lecture. "Listen. Chasing it will lose more. Reporting it fast gives the police a chance. And she'd rather hear it from you now than find out later."
That evening Pranav filed a complaint with the cyber police, and the regulator. Then he went home and told his wife.

I'm Mridul, and for two months I hid the worst mistake of my life from my sister Irawati.
We shared a flat. I had put ₹2 lakh, all my savings plus some of our shared emergency fund, into an "AI trading" app a friend recommended. It showed profits every day. Then it froze. Customer support said I had to pay a "release fee" to withdraw.
I paid the fee. Then another. I told myself if I could just get it back, Irawati would never need to know.
Every time she asked why I looked so tired, I said "work." I stopped eating properly. I felt like a fraud in my own home.
One night she found me sitting on the kitchen floor at 3 a.m. She sat down next to me and waited.
I told her everything. She didn't shout. She said, "We report it tomorrow. And no more fees." We went to the cyber police in the morning. I wish I'd told her on day one.
